extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, mass-communication researchers, and graduate students
extracted.subtask_description: Formulating, organizing, and testing assumptions, propositions, and hypotheses about how multiple levels of influence (individuals, routines, organizations, extramedia forces, ideology) shape media/news content and its effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish exposure to medium from exposure to specific content
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure to a medium is not equivalent to exposure to specific content within that medium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers must collect more information in effects studies about what a person has been exposed to; measuring hours of TV or days reading a paper can conflate many content types (e.g., comics vs. public affairs), and heavy viewing does not guarantee exposure to particular content (e.g., violent shows).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for cyclical/temporal variation in media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Media content varies day by day and occurs in cycles; content on one day is not necessarily equivalent to content on another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: newspaper page counts vary by weekday; governmental/business sources are less available between Friday noon and Monday noon, reducing available news items. Effects studies should identify and control for these cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop content-analysis measures that are reliable and valid across content kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Content analysis measures must be standardized and valid across many kinds of content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standardization of content analysis lags behind survey/experimental methods; without more sophisticated measures, different messages may appear identical under current measures while differing in important ways (e.g., two shows with same violence score may differ in other attributes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess audience awareness of influences on media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the extent to which audiences are aware (correctly or not) of factors that influence media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience perceptions (e.g., knowledge that a publisher has business ties) may change how they interpret content and alter effects (e.g., voting against a recommended candidate because of perceived bias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify relative importance and contingent conditions of influences on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all influences on content are equally important; determine which influences are crucial contingent conditions for the effects being studied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some influences (e.g., media routines, individual behavior, organizational factors, ideological forces) may dominate in different contexts; link organizational factors to larger power centers to understand origins of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume mass media content is socially constructed
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass media content is a socially created product, not a reflection of an objective reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although stimulus may be a real-world event, many factors determine what is transmitted and how it is treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize intentional and unintentional influences on content
rubrics_metrics.description: Some influences on content are intentional and others occur as a result of other actions (e.g., bias in favor of certain sources may occur because those sources are more available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Availability of sources (e.g., corporations) can create systematic biases irrespective of deliberate intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content understanding is crucial to understanding media effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding the nature of media content is crucial to understanding the nature and importance of content's effects on people and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without content-specific measures, effects studies risk ignoring important causal connections between exposure and effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer influences from content attributes
rubrics_metrics.description: From media content we can infer many of the factors that shaped it (e.g., language reveals writer attitudes; story selection reveals editor priorities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Content attributes can serve as indicators of individual, organizational, or ideological influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: General forces shape news and entertainment similarly
rubrics_metrics.description: The general forces operating to shape news content also shape entertainment content; both are influenced by individual media workers, routines, organizations, extramedia factors, and ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influences can be ranked hierarchically
rubrics_metrics.description: Influences on media content can be ranked hierarchically from macrosystem-level (ideology/culture) down to micro-level (individual worker characteristics), with each level subject to limits set by higher levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example chain: role conceptions derive from socialization to routines; routines exist to meet organizational standards/goals; standards are set by advertisers, audiences, market economy; these stem from ideological/cultural imperatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gatekeeping limits what becomes media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Not everything eligible to be mass media content actually gets into the media; gatekeeping selects items from the universe of possible ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: not every film idea becomes a film; not every event is covered in news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media routines develop to increase efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Media routines developed as a way to make the media worker's job more efficient and to meet audience expectations and source constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routines structure how information is handled and presented (e.g., deadlines, inverted pyramid, objectivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners hold ultimate power in media organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate power in a media organization comes from the owner; owners set direction and ultimate policies, though lower-level employees exert influence too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners can hire/fire and influence both editorial and news content directly and indirectly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media control occurs via financial and regulatory mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: All mass media are controlled in one way or another; control is exerted through media financing, and in government-owned media control is direct, while in private media control is indirect via laws, regulations, licenses, taxes, and ideological direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television contains consistently high levels of violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Television content (news and entertainment) contains a high level of violence that is consistent over time; when crimes are depicted they are more likely violent than nonviolent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program-to-program fluctuations exist but the overall picture shows substantial violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Underrepresentation and stereotyped portrayal of women and aged
rubrics_metrics.description: Women and the aged appear less often than men and younger adults and are presented differently (e.g., two-thirds of TV characters are male; women shown younger/inferior roles; women more often victims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aged are treated stereotypically with age as primary attribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: News favors already prominent people
rubrics_metrics.description: Most news concerns people already prominent; nonprominent people must do something deviant to receive coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official sources dominate news content
rubrics_metrics.description: Most news comes from 'official' (primarily governmental) channels; journalists use other sources when available but official and business sources are most accessible and often prepare information specifically for journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual or small-group sources are less accessible and less skilled in media relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic biases in state coverage (U.S. example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States, news coverage of a state is not related to its population: Pacific and Atlantic coast states are overcovered relative to population, Midwest states undercovered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television overrepresents high-status occupational characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Among television characters, more people with high-status jobs are shown than low-status jobs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minorities underrepresented and stereotyped; coverage reflects power relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Minority characters and newscasters are generally underrepresented and portrayed stereotypically; portrayals reflect the power relations of society, with white characters shown as more powerful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More acculturated and higher socio-economic minorities receive more prominent coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational background of media workers influences content
rubrics_metrics.description: Media workers who have a 'communication' college degree produce content with different characteristics than those with other majors; employer preferences reflect assumptions about educational preparation for journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some employers prefer journalism majors; others prefer liberal arts such as American Studies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual background affects content proportionate to power
rubrics_metrics.description: A journalist's background and personal characteristics will affect media content in proportion to the amount of power the person holds within the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions occur when assignments are made by ethnicity or other institutional considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity between journalist and subjects affects coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: People similar to a journalist will be covered differently than those who are dissimilar; demographic characteristics of the communicator affect content, especially when reporting about members of the communicator's own demographic group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: women write about women differently than men; Hispanics cover Hispanic community differently than Anglos; sexual orientation can influence story framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal attitudes affect content when power and weak routines permit
rubrics_metrics.description: Media workers' personal attitudes affect the content they produce, contingent on having sufficient power to influence production and on the absence of strong routines covering the task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists have leeway in selection of words/visuals; sports announcers, filmmakers, publishers can reflect personal prejudices/values in content and project choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' role conceptions shape coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists' role conceptions (interpreting, disseminating information, adversary of the powerful) determine job definitions, what should be covered, and how stories are covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived ethics reduce unethical actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The more unethical media workers think an action is, the less likely they are to take part in it; lack of required ethical code results in disagreement about what is ethical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenure socializes workers to organizational policies
rubrics_metrics.description: The longer people work for a media organization, the more socialized they are to its stated and unstated policies; workers learn organizational wants by observing others and receiving feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socialization includes observing what makes it into the finished product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity routine suppresses individual opinion in straight news
rubrics_metrics.description: Media workers are less likely to insert their own value judgments into straight news accounts than into features or entertainment; the routine of objectivity overrules individual tendency to inject opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines increase likelihood content will be used
rubrics_metrics.description: The more media workers follow organizational routines, the more likely their content is to be used; routines (gatekeeping, deadlines, inverted pyramid, objectivity) shape selection and presentation of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If routines were different, content would differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning routines yields professional reinforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The more media workers learn job routines, the more they are rated professional by co-workers; following established procedures receives positive reinforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communicators' jobs require handling lots of information; routine procedures ease that task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual factors dominate on topics without established routines
rubrics_metrics.description: On stories or subjects without established routines, especially in early stages of an issue, individual factors will be relatively more influential compared with routines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routines supersede individual influence on well-established story types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events congruent with routines are more likely covered
rubrics_metrics.description: Events that are congruent with media routines are more likely to be covered than discongruent events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: news off the journalist's beat may go unreported; events lacking good film/video may be dropped from TV newscasts; press conferences before deadlines more likely covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events are more likely covered than issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Events are more likely to be covered than issues because events are easier to defend as news and covering events has become a routine in journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage consistency and pack journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: News organizations value consistency over time; the more journalists cover an event the more similar their coverage will be (pack journalism), as journalists read/view others' work for confirmation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors question coverage different from other organizations, encouraging homogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful/successful actors receive more negative coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The more powerful or successful people or groups are, the more negative news coverage of them will be; coverage of front-runners and incumbents tends to be more negative than toward underdogs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Looking for flaws in potential winners is routine investigative behavior; journalists may be magnanimous toward losers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational size/complexity shifts influence toward management
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger and more complex a media organization is, the less influence professional routines will have and the more influence larger organizational forces (economic concerns, bureaucracy) will have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More layers of bureaucracy distance top management from reporters; top management bases decisions on economic concerns and intervenes only if routines threaten organization goals; resource constraints push routines favoring efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite media organizations hire less demographically representative staff
rubrics_metrics.description: The more elite a medium is, the less similar its workers will be to the general population; elite organizations tend to hire people from more elite backgrounds and journalists at elite outlets are more liberal on average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational economic health conditions profit-driven content decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which an organization's need to make a profit affects media content is contingent on the overall economic health of the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizations making satisfactory profit permit professional influences over economic ones; organizations at economic risk prioritize profit over professional considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast media more sensitive to advertisers than print
rubrics_metrics.description: Television and radio are more sensitive to the need to make a profit than newspapers and magazines because virtually all TV/radio income derives from advertisers and programming decisions have direct market consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every programming decision has economic ramifications in broadcast media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business-background managers favor economic decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Upper-level management personnel with business backgrounds are more likely to make decisions based on economics rather than professional considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle management mediates between business and editorial pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: Middle-level management personnel are more closely attuned to organizational goals than lower-level staff, and editors may be more sensitive to the business side, bringing reporters and editors into conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: When business and editorial conflict, business can dominate if combined control exists
rubrics_metrics.description: When editorial routines conflict with the need to make a profit, if the editor controls both business and editorial sides, the editorial side will be given lower priority because business concerns seem more concrete and immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher-ranked individuals have more nonmedia connections
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher an individual is in a media organization, the more likely he or she is to have connections with nonmedia organizations (boards, civic groups).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such connections can affect editorial policies and coverage priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Owners' attitudes can subtly shape coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The personal attitudes and values of news media owners may be reflected not only in editorials but also in news and features; employees try to anticipate owner preferences causing subtle 'slants'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners can hire/fire editors, columnists, reporters according to beliefs; this shapes both overt and tacit content norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absentee ownership reduces local aggressive coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The further the owner lives from the organization, the less local news, editorials, and features the organization transmits; absentee owners are less likely to adopt aggressive local coverage and more likely to follow corporate policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absentee ownership common among companies owning multiple media outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain ownership weakens community attachment of workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Media workers from chain-owned organizations form weaker attachments to the local community than workers for independent organizations; loyalty may be more to corporation than community and employees may move across outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chain organizations show homogeneous political endorsements and centralized personnel rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Chain organizations are more likely to endorse presidential candidates homogeneously across the chain; promotions and salary increases go to employees who perform, but higher workers' rewards are more affected by chain administrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homogeneity may result from convergence of editorial views rather than overt collusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources adapting to routines gain favorable coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The more sources know about and adapt to a media organization's routines (timing, formatting, preferred form), the more likely they are to get favorable coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sources that deliver news releases in the form and time the media prefer are most likely to get coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising volume affects amount of editorial space
rubrics_metrics.description: The more advertising a newspaper or magazine has, the more pages it will devote to editorial (nonadvertising) content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Print media assume a percentage of pages will be advertising and editorial fills the remainder; if ads increase, total pages often increase, allowing more editorial space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extramedia–media connections amplify extramedia influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The more connections there are between extramedia organizations and media organizations, the more influence extramedia firms will have over content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pressure can be exerted through upper-level management connections between media and nonmedia companies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powerful sources exert more influence via resources and PR staff
rubrics_metrics.description: The more economic or political power a source has, the more likely he or she is to influence news reports; such sources have accessible staff who provide quick, concise information to media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful sources' infrastructure aids their media influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official sources dominate more in issue stories than event stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Although official sources dominate most news content, the percentage of official sources is higher in issue stories than in event stories because issues involve vested interests of official actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest-group criticism induces self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: The more critical an interest group is of media coverage, the more likely the media are to self-censor; interest groups influence content via publicity and by targeting advertisers for boycotts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Media may anticipate complaints and alter coverage preemptively or comply with requested changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slow news days increase PR-generated content
rubrics_metrics.description: The slower the news day, the more likely media content is to be generated by public-relations practitioners and interest groups, who provide events and new information for coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists still need to fill preset amounts of news content even without big events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite media agenda-setting influences other media
rubrics_metrics.description: The more coverage elite, opinion-leading media give an issue or event, the more likely other media are to give subsequent coverage; elite outlets serve as agenda setters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists read each other's stories and watch each other's newscasts, amplifying lead coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience-target promotion shapes content orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: The more a media organization promotes itself within a target audience, the more its content will reflect the interests of that audience; outlets may abandon mass audiences for deep penetration of advertiser-attractive segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television programming depends on ratings showing audience characteristics; unattractive audiences may lead to program abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertisers shape and constrain media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers influence media content: when advertisers support one kind of content more, media offer more of it; advertisers can threaten or withdraw support to delete or shape objectionable content and can create content to showcase products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertiser preferences and economic power directly condition media offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government tries to control media when criticized
rubrics_metrics.description: The more the mass media criticize a country's government, the more the government will try to control the media through financing, laws, regulations, court cases, licenses, taxes, information manipulation, and direct communication with managers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Source and interest-group criticism of the media also prompt government control attempts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community characteristics influence media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of the community in which a medium operates may influence its content: larger markets show more spontaneous news events and local news; presence of a competing newspaper does not necessarily increase content diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic breadth standardizes content
rubrics_metrics.description: The wider the geographic area a medium covers, the more standardized its content will be, because messages must appeal broadly and thus take fewer chances and innovate less.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviance increases inclusion and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: The more deviant people or events are, the more likely they are to be included in media content and the more likely they are to be stereotyped; media maintain social order by showing approved vs. disapproved behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deviant actors/events may be trivialized or shown as dangerous; applies across domestic and foreign coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: International significance conditions foreign coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The more political, economic, or cultural significance one country has for another, the more the former will appear in the latter's mass media; system-level attachments affect priorities in coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with similar news values, measures of significance affect perceived importance and newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity routines not used where consensus exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists will not use objective routines (such as balance) when subjects are outside legitimate controversy and lie in areas of consensus or deviance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elites act collectively when ideological principles threatened
rubrics_metrics.description: Elites will respond to media as a class when core ideological principles are threatened; actions of business or elites will be more unified and coordinated when capitalist values are under attack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite connections produce ideological consistency in content
rubrics_metrics.description: The more closely media are connected to other elites (board interlocks, club memberships), the more media content will be consistent with elite ideological viewpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupational-paradigm violations are repaired to preserve paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of occupational paradigms (anomalies) must be repaired to preserve the paradigm, especially when violations cross important ideological boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repair mechanisms defend professional/ideological order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television more ideologically charged than print on issues
rubrics_metrics.description: On a given issue, television coverage will be more ideologically charged than print media coverage.
